target: AG1's claim that animal dissection should be used because it provides valuable hands-on biology learning and skill development
objection: Animal dissection is not educationally necessary because biology education goals can be met without it: it is not required by AP Biology or NGSS, and non-animal alternatives such as synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the relevant content at least as well.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is a productive use of dead animals and avoids major harm because the animals are already deceased or are byproducts
objection: The ethical-cost premise is wrong in practice: most dissection animals are reportedly caught in the wild, so the activity still involves inhumane sourcing and environmental harm even if some specimens are described as already dead or byproducts.

target: AG2's claim that dissection typically involves inhumane wild-capture and biodiversity loss
objection: AG2's ethical-harm argument assumes the animals are wild-caught, but AG1 says typical classroom specimens are already deceased or food-industry byproducts, so the wild-capture and biodiversity-loss harms AG2 relies on are not the relevant harms for those dissections.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives are just as good and dissection is unnecessary
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations do not require students to cut and manipulate real tissues or work with actual anatomical structures, so they cannot replicate the same depth of fine-motor, hand-eye coordination, and real-specimen observation/analysis training as dissection.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is justified because byproduct/deceased sourcing avoids the main ethical harms
objection: Even if the animal is dead by the time of dissection, that does not erase harms that happened earlier during wild capture; therefore the claim that byproduct or already-deceased specimens avoid the relevant ethical and environmental harms is false in practice.

target: AG2's claim that only required curricula or physician training matter for judging whether dissection is worthwhile
objection: A school science practice can still be educationally justified even if it is not required by AP/NGSS or used in physician training, because those standards are not the only measure of educational value.

target: AG1's claim that typical dissection animals are already deceased or byproducts, so the harms are minimal
objection: Most dissection animals are still reportedly wild-caught, so the byproduct/already-deceased framing does not reflect how dissection programs typically source specimens and does not eliminate the underlying ethical and biodiversity harms.

target: AG1's claim that dissection can be done with minimal incremental harm because the animals are already dead or byproducts
objection: The harm-minimization argument fails because the supply chain still typically involves wild capture, which causes inhumane treatment and biodiversity loss; thus the activity still carries substantial ethical and ecological costs.

target: AG2's claim that wild-capture harms are the basis for banning dissection
objection: AG1 argues that classroom dissection commonly uses already-deceased or meat-industry byproduct animals, so the wild-capture and biodiversity-loss harms AG2 emphasizes are not the operative harms in those implementations.

target: AG1's claim that already-deceased/byproduct sourcing removes the relevant harms
objection: Being already dead at the time of classroom use does not erase the prior harms of wild capture, so the byproduct/already-deceased framing does not eliminate the ethical and environmental damage associated with sourcing dissection animals.

target: AG1's claim that byproduct/deceased sourcing means dissection does not impose substantial harms
objection: In typical dissection programs, around 99% of animals are said to be wild-caught, so assuming byproduct or already-deceased procurement does not remove the substantial sourcing harms that dissection can impose.

target: AG1's claim that school dissection usually uses already-deceased/byproduct specimens rather than wild-caught animals
objection: Because approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, classroom dissection typically depends on wild-capture rather than only on byproducts, so the relevant harms are not avoided.

target: AG2's claim that the sourcing harms remain substantial in typical school dissection
objection: AG1 counters that typical school specimens are meat-industry byproducts and already deceased, so the wild-capture and biodiversity-loss harms AG2 describes are not the operative harms for those classroom implementations.

target: AG1's claim that byproduct/already-deceased procurement removes the relevant harms
objection: Even when procurement is framed as byproduct-based, the actual supply of dissection animals reportedly still relies on wild capture in most cases, so the relevant harms are not removed.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is unnecessary because alternatives meet the learning objectives and there is no medical justification
objection: Real animal dissection gives students tactile, hands-on experience with real tissues and specimen-based anatomy that alternatives do not match, so it can provide educational benefits that make it necessary rather than unnecessary.

target: AG1's claim that alternatives do not teach the relevant skills as well as dissection
objection: Well-designed synthetic models and simulations can include tool-based, hands-on practice, can be reused for repeated repetitions, and can create engagement and 'aha' moments, so dissection does not provide a unique educational mechanism or superior learning outcomes.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives can match dissection on hands-on learning
objection: Although alternatives can be interactive, they cannot reproduce the authentic tactile response and real anatomical variability of biological tissues, so they do not match the adaptive fine-motor and specimen-based reasoning that real dissection teaches.
